I use power to weight ratio to judge a cars potential, but its only potential. There are so many variables in play. Gearing, transmission type, how power is made, power curve, tires it goes on endlessly. Just as a rule of thumb think of it this way. Most factory vehicles, just ordinary cars, fall somewhere around 20-23:1 power to weight ratio. Thats 20-23 pounds per horsepower. Thats kind of the mundane belt. But there are other factors, like torque and gearing.  Generally a manual transmission is better than a traditional automatic and a traditional automatic is better than a CVT. Also some vehicles, like diesels and especially turbo diesels make little power but a lot of torque. A diesel hatchback is as fast as a sportier version from 0-45ish, than falls off because it doesn't have the horsepower numbers to keep up. Than there is the actual weight to consider. A 6000 pound vehicle with a 10:1 power to weight ratio will accelerate very quickly, but its still a 3 ton car and may struggle in the corners and under braking. Where as a 2300 pound car with a 17:1 ratio won't accelerate all that quickly, but is leaps and bounds better at braking and cornering. This is one of the reasons small sports cars and older sedans are so popular. Last is how power is made. So take a baseline 300HP. Look at an older muscle car, a turbocharged compact and lets say an old luxury grand tourer. Thats a naturally aspirated V8, a turbo charged H4 and a supercharged I6. The NA-V8 will be very responsive and have a very natural torque curve making for good acceleration. The Turbo will take longer to spool up and build power (less true with newer and newer vehicles) and suffer the risk of losing boost with speed changes. The supercharger will be more similar to the NA-V8 with a linear torque curve but loses some initial power to parasitic loss.  All this info is great to have and learn more about but in the end the only reliable test of whether a car does what you want it to do is to drive it and see. The only benchmark is the seat of your pants.

I hated my Dad when I was a kid, absolutely despised him, cause he never made it easy. I wanted little to do with him and swore I would never be anything like him. It wasn't until I became a parent that I began to appreciate what that really meant. He taught me, forced me really, to hold myself to a higher standard. Taught me about self-respect, honor, discipline. Doing the right thing for it's own sake, not for fear of reprisals, nor for what rewards there may be. He taught me how to be true to myself and to constantly seek to better myself. He was an under educated Vet, got his diploma in the Army, barely and supported his family with the strength of his back. He always worked more hours then he slept. But he still found time to attend classes whenever we could afford it and to consume books constantly. Never fiction, only historical or educational texts. In his fifties this man could out work anyone on site. He could fix anything, build anything and debate anything. He taught me to turn wrenches, taught me to how to lay beads, but also taught me critical thinking and the value of education and intelligence. He passed away two Decembers ago. He turned 60, about a week later was diagnosed with Liver cancer. He spent the next six months fighting like hell and reassuring all of *us* that it was going to be ok. That he was proud of us all, and loved us all and that he had made peace with this world. He had bought a home in the hills like he had always promised to do. He had descendants like he always wanted and they knew him and would remember him. So he was okay with whatever happened. When he died it seemed like a relief for him, but we're all still standing around sort of shell shocked. I sort of laugh now whenever I think back to angsty little rebel me when I was a kid and how much I fucking hated my Dad. I was such a dickweed, but my Dad knew what it was like and he never made it easy for me. I'm sure it would have been easier for him to just let me be the little asshole I seemed so bent on being. But he didn't and now whenever anyone tells me I'm so much like him, I couldn't be happier.
